items.stem: Here is a student's answer to the question “Describe the League's humanitarian work in the 1920s.” [4]: “The ILO campaigned for better working conditions. It was very important and affected a lot of people.” Using the mark scheme (one mark per relevant point, a further mark for supporting detail), how many marks would you award? Explain your decision and suggest how the answer could be improved.
items.answer: 1 mark: 1 relevant point with no further development; the general sentence gains no credit. To improve, add further precise points such as: About 400,000 prisoners of war were returned home. The Refugee Committee helped refugees, for example with Nansen passports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct mark (1/4); 1 mark for explaining why the other sentences gain no credit; 1 mark for a valid improvement with accurate detail [3]

items.stem: Here is a student's answer to the question “Describe the membership of the League of Nations in the 1920s and 1930s.” [4]: “Germany was excluded at first and joined in 1926. Britain and France were the most powerful members throughout. The USA never joined. It was very important and affected a lot of people.” Using the mark scheme (one mark per relevant point, a further mark for supporting detail), how many marks would you award? Explain your decision and suggest how the answer could be improved.
items.answer: 3 marks: 3 relevant points with no further development; the general sentence gains no credit. To improve, add further precise points such as: Bolshevik Russia was excluded; the USSR joined only in 1934. Japan and Germany left in 1933 and Italy in 1937.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct mark (3/4); 1 mark for explaining why the other sentences gain no credit; 1 mark for a valid improvement with accurate detail [3]

items.stem: Paper 1 (a)-style question. What were the terms of the Nazi-Soviet Pact?
items.answer: Germany and the USSR promised not to attack each other for ten years. They agreed not to help any enemy of the other. A secret protocol divided Poland between them. The USSR would have a sphere of influence over the Baltic states and Bessarabia. A separate trade agreement gave Germany Soviet raw materials.

They agreed not to help any enemy of the other. A secret protocol divided Poland between them. The USSR would have a sphere of influence over the Baltic states and Bessarabia. A separate trade agreement gave Germany Soviet raw materials. [4]

items.stem: Practise your (a) technique. Describe the rise of Solidarity in Poland in 1980-81.
items.answer: Rising food prices led to strikes, including at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk in August 1980. Strikers led by Lech Wałęsa issued 21 demands, including free trade unions and the right to strike. The government accepted the Gdańsk Agreement in August 1980. Solidarity grew to about ten million members. In December 1981 General Jaruzelski declared martial law and banned Solidarity.

Solidarity grew to about ten million members. In December 1981 General Jaruzelski declared martial law and banned Solidarity. [4]

items.stem: A student has made these notes to answer the question “Describe the consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis.” P: The USA secretly removed its Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Q: Germany and the USSR promised not to attack each other for ten years. R: A hotline was set up between Washington and Moscow in 1963. S: No more secret treaties (open diplomacy). T: Khrushchev's reputation was damaged and he was removed in 1964. U: He wanted to end the threat of the German navy to Britain. (a) Identify which notes are relevant to the question. (b) Explain why the other notes would gain no credit. (c) Use the relevant notes to write a four-mark answer, adding supporting detail.
items.answer: (a) P, R, T. (b) The others are accurate but about different topics, so they do not answer the question. (c) The Soviet missiles were removed from Cuba. The USA secretly removed its Jupiter missiles from Turkey. A hotline was set up between Washington and Moscow in 1963. The Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed in 1963. Castro remained in power and Cuba stayed communist. Khrushchev's reputation was damaged and he was removed in 1964.
items.markingKey: (a) P, R, T [1] (b) explanation of relevance [1] (c) One mark for each relevant point; a further mark for supporting detail, up to 4 marks. items.stem: Consider the question “Why did the USA introduce the Marshall Plan?” Here are some reasons: P: It would strengthen the policy of containment begun with the Truman Doctrine. Q: Poverty could make communism attractive, as in Italy and France where communist parties were strong. R: A prosperous Europe would buy American goods and help the US economy. Explain how each reason contributed, show how at least two of them were linked, and decide which was the most important. Justify your choice.
items.answer: Explains each reason in turn; links, for example, how one reason made another more serious; reaches a judgement on the most important reason with criteria (e.g. which made the outcome certain, or which came first and caused the others).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): describes reasons. Level 2 (3-5): explains reasons separately. Level 3 (6-8): explains and links reasons. Level 4 (9-10): explains and links reasons and reaches a supported judgement on relative importance [10]

items.stem: Study Source A, President Kennedy's speech in West Berlin, 26 June 1963 (summary with extracts). Kennedy told a huge crowd that “all free men, wherever they may live, are citizens of Berlin, and, therefore, as a free man, I take pride in the words ‘Ich bin ein Berliner’.” He said the Wall showed the failures of the communist system. Explain the difference between the message of Source A and its purpose, using details of the source.
items.answer: Message: Kennedy presents the Wall as evidence that communism had failed and that West Berlin stood for freedom. Purpose: To reassure West Berliners of US support and to win a propaganda victory over the USSR.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid message supported by a detail; 1 mark for a valid purpose linked to the author, audience or date; up to 2 marks for explaining the difference (what it says vs why it was produced) [4]

The country voted for the League; it did not vote for this.” Use your own knowledge to explain one thing about the League's handling of Manchuria and Abyssinia that Source A does not tell us.
items.answer: That the French government also supported the plan, and Mussolini's determination to conquer.

items.stem: Source skills practice. Study Source A, a cartoon by David Low titled “Rendezvous”, published in the British newspaper the Evening Standard, 20 September 1939. Hitler and Stalin meet over the body of a dead soldier representing Poland. They bow politely to each other. Hitler says: “The scum of the earth, I believe?” Stalin replies: “The bloody assassin of the workers, I presume?” (a) How reliable is Source A as an account of the Nazi-Soviet Pact? Explain your answer. [6] (b) Use your own knowledge to explain one thing about the Nazi-Soviet Pact that Source A does not tell us. [3]
items.answer: (a) Reliable because Low was a well-informed cartoonist and the cartoon was published at the time. Less reliable because it is a satirical comment by a British critic of both dictators. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view on the Nazi-Soviet Pact, but it needs cross-checking with other evidence. (b) That Stalin had tried, and failed, to reach an agreement with Britain and France in 1939.
items.markingKey: (a) Level 1 (1): generic comment (e.g. "it is biased"). Level 2 (2-3): reliability judged on content or type only. Level 3 (4-5): explains reliability using the author, date and purpose. Level 4 (6): reaches a balanced judgement using provenance and cross-reference with own knowledge. [6] (b) 1 mark for a relevant point from own knowledge; up to 2 further marks for development and explaining why it matters [3]

items.stem: Source skills practice: cross-referencing. Source A: an extract from a modern history textbook (illustrative). “Gorbachev did not set out to end Soviet control of eastern Europe. But once it was clear that Soviet tanks would not come, the communist regimes, which had depended on that threat for forty years, fell within months.” Source B: a list of the main demands of the Gdańsk strikers, August 1980 (summary of selected demands). The strikers demanded free trade unions independent of the Communist Party, the right to strike, freedom of speech and the press, the release of political prisoners and the broadcasting of Sunday Mass on the radio. (a) What can you infer from each source about the collapse of Soviet control in eastern Europe? [4] (b) How far do Sources A and B agree? [7] (c) Which source is more useful to a historian studying the collapse of Soviet control in eastern Europe? Explain your answer using the provenance of both sources. [7]
items.answer: (a) A: It argues Gorbachev's refusal to use force was decisive, even though he did not intend the collapse. B: It shows the strikers wanted political freedoms, not just better pay and conditions. (b) They disagree about whether Gorbachev was the main reason for the collapse of Soviet control in eastern Europe. (c) A: it is written with hindsight and can draw on later evidence; but it is a brief summary and plays down economic and popular causes. B: it shows exactly what the strikers asked for; but it does not show how many Poles supported these demands or how the government responded. Judgement depends on the enquiry; each is useful for different purposes.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks for each valid inference supported from the source [4] (b) Level 1 (1): undeveloped comparison. Level 2 (2-3): compares content, agreement OR disagreement, with details. Level 3 (4-5): compares agreement AND disagreement with details. Level 4 (6-7): compares the overall messages / points of view, supported, and explains why they differ (provenance). [7] (c) Level 1 (1): undeveloped or generic comment. Level 2 (2-3): useful or not useful based on face-value content. Level 3 (4-5): uses content checked against own knowledge. Level 4 (6-7): evaluates the provenance (author, audience, purpose, date) to judge usefulness. [7]

items.stem: Source skills practice: cross-referencing. Source A: figures from the economic historian C. P. Kindleberger, The World in Depression (1973), based on League of Nations data. “Total monthly imports of 75 countries (millions of US gold dollars): January 1929: 2,998; January 1930: 2,739; January 1931: 1,839; January 1932: 1,206; January 1933: 992.” Source B: an article in a Japanese newspaper, 1931 (illustrative). “Our farmers are ruined since America stopped buying our silk. Manchuria, with its coal, iron and land, is Japan's lifeline. The government must act.” (a) What can you infer from each source about the effects of the Depression on international relations? [4] (b) How far do Sources A and B agree? [7] (c) Which source is more useful to a historian studying the effects of the Depression on international relations? Explain your answer using the provenance of both sources. [7]
items.answer: (a) A: It shows world trade fell by about two-thirds between January 1929 and January 1933. B: It shows economic hardship led many Japanese to support expansion into Manchuria. (b) They broadly agree about whether the Depression was the main reason the League failed in the 1930s. (c) A: statistics based on League data allow comparison over time; but the figures are totals and do not show how different countries were affected. B: it reflects views that were common in Japan in 1931; but it is written to persuade and does not mention the army's own ambitions. Judgement depends on the enquiry; each is useful for different purposes.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks for each valid inference supported from the source [4] (b) Level 1 (1): undeveloped comparison. Level 2 (2-3): compares content, agreement OR disagreement, with details. Level 3 (4-5): compares agreement AND disagreement with details. Level 4 (6-7): compares the overall messages / points of view, supported, and explains why they differ (provenance). [7] (c) Level 1 (1): undeveloped or generic comment. Level 2 (2-3): useful or not useful based on face-value content. Level 3 (4-5): uses content checked against own knowledge. Level 4 (6-7): evaluates the provenance (author, audience, purpose, date) to judge usefulness. [7]

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “You may strip Germany of her colonies, reduce her armaments to a mere police force and her navy to that of a fifth-rate power; all the same in the end if she feels that she has been unjustly treated in the peace of 1919 she will find means of exacting retribution from her conquerors.” (Lloyd George's Fontainebleau Memorandum, a paper written for the other peacemakers in March 1919 (abridged).) Explain the difference between the message of Source A and its purpose, using details of the source.
items.answer: Message: Lloyd George warns that a treaty Germany sees as unjust will lead to German revenge, however weak Germany is made. Purpose: To persuade Clemenceau and Wilson to moderate the terms, especially on territory and reparations.

items.stem: Paper 1 (c)-style question. By the end of 1968 there were over half a million American troops in Vietnam. ‘The tactics of the Viet Cong were the main reason why the USA failed in Vietnam.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Guerrilla warfare and tunnels neutralised American firepower. The Ho Chi Minh Trail kept them supplied. They won support from many villagers. Against: US tactics such as search and destroy alienated the population. The South Vietnamese government was corrupt and unpopular. Opposition grew in the USA, especially after Tet in 1968. North Vietnam received aid from China and the USSR. Judgement: Viet Cong tactics were crucial, but they succeeded because US methods and an unpopular South Vietnamese government made it impossible to win support.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1): general answer. Level 2 (2-3): identifies and/or describes. Level 3 (4-6): explains one side. Level 4 (7-9): explains both sides. Level 5 (10): explains both sides and reaches a supported judgement on "how far" / "how important". Agree / supporting: Guerrilla warfare and tunnels neutralised American firepower. The Ho Chi Minh Trail kept them supplied. They won support from many villagers. Disagree / other factors: US tactics such as search and destroy alienated the population. The South Vietnamese government was corrupt and unpopular. Opposition grew in the USA, especially after Tet in 1968. North Vietnam received aid from China and the USSR. Possible judgement: Viet Cong tactics were crucial, but they succeeded because US methods and an unpopular South Vietnamese government made it impossible to win support. [10]

items.stem: Consider the question “Why did the West see Soviet actions in eastern Europe as a threat?” Here are some reasons: P: Communist rule was imposed by force and opponents were persecuted. Q: Communist parties were strong in western Europe, for example in France and Italy, and in Greece there was a civil war. R: Soviet control seemed to show communist expansion was under way, as Churchill's Iron Curtain speech warned. Explain how each reason contributed, show how at least two of them were linked, and decide which was the most important. Justify your choice.
items.answer: Explains each reason in turn; links, for example, how one reason made another more serious; reaches a judgement on the most important reason with criteria (e.g. which made the outcome certain, or which came first and caused the others).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): describes reasons. Level 2 (3-5): explains reasons separately. Level 3 (6-8): explains and links reasons. Level 4 (9-10): explains and links reasons and reaches a supported judgement on relative importance [10]

Q: He distrusted Britain and France after they excluded him from Munich. R: The pact gave him land in Poland and the Baltic states as a buffer zone. Explain how each reason contributed, show how at least two of them were linked, and decide which was the most important. Justify your choice.
items.answer: Explains each reason in turn; links, for example, how one reason made another more serious; reaches a judgement on the most important reason with criteria (e.g. which made the outcome certain, or which came first and caused the others).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): describes reasons. Level 2 (3-5): explains reasons separately. Level 3 (6-8): explains and links reasons. Level 4 (9-10): explains and links reasons and reaches a supported judgement on relative importance [10]

items.stem: Study Source A, a photograph taken for the Associated Press near Trang Bang, South Vietnam, June 1972 (description). Children run screaming along a road after a napalm attack. In the centre is a nine-year-old girl, Phan Thi Kim Phuc, whose clothes have been burnt off. Soldiers walk behind them. Explain the difference between the message of Source A and its purpose, using details of the source.
items.answer: Message: It shows the terrible suffering of Vietnamese civilians caused by the war. Purpose: To record the effects of the napalm attack; when published around the world it increased opposition to the war.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid message supported by a detail; 1 mark for a valid purpose linked to the author, audience or date; up to 2 marks for explaining the difference (what it says vs why it was produced) [4]

items.stem: Study Source A, a cartoon of the kind published in British newspapers in 1923 (illustrative description). The cartoon shows a large figure representing Mussolini standing over a small figure representing Greece. Figures representing the League of Nations look on, uncertain what to do. Explain the difference between the message of Source A and its purpose, using details of the source.
items.answer: Message: It suggests the League was powerless when a strong country like Italy bullied a weak one. Purpose: To criticise the League and the Great Powers for allowing Mussolini to get his way.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid message supported by a detail; 1 mark for a valid purpose linked to the author, audience or date; up to 2 marks for explaining the difference (what it says vs why it was produced) [4]

items.stem: Source skills practice. Source D is an extract from a book by an American historian writing in the late 1960s (illustrative of the revisionist view). “American leaders wanted an open world for American trade and investment. They saw Soviet security needs in eastern Europe as aggression and used their atomic monopoly to try to force Stalin to give way.” Study the source. Use your own knowledge to explain one thing about responsibility for the Cold War that Source D does not tell us.
items.answer: Soviet use of force and rigged elections in eastern Europe.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a relevant point from own knowledge; up to 2 further marks for development and explaining why it matters [3]

items.stem: Source skills practice: cross-referencing. Source A: a speech by Winston Churchill at Fulton, Missouri, 5 March 1946 (extract). “From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.” Source B: Stalin's response to Churchill's Fulton speech, published in the Soviet newspaper Pravda, March 1946 (summary). Stalin said that the USSR had lost far more people than Britain and the USA together in the war, and that it was natural for it to want governments friendly to the USSR in the countries through which Germany had attacked. He compared Churchill to Hitler as a warmonger. (a) What can you infer from each source about the Soviet takeover of eastern Europe? [4] (b) How far do Sources A and B agree? [7] (c) Which source is more useful to a historian studying the Soviet takeover of eastern Europe? Explain your answer using the provenance of both sources. [7]
items.answer: (a) A: Churchill warns that Europe has been divided and that eastern Europe is now cut off under Soviet control. B: Stalin argues that Soviet control of eastern Europe was a natural defensive response to the war. (b) They disagree about whether Stalin's actions in eastern Europe were mainly defensive. (c) A: Churchill was a respected wartime leader with knowledge of events; but he was out of office and strongly anti-communist, speaking to persuade the USA to act. B: it gives Stalin's own justification; but it is propaganda in a state-controlled newspaper and ignores how communists were seizing power. Judgement depends on the enquiry; each is useful for different purposes.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks for each valid inference supported from the source [4] (b) Level 1 (1): undeveloped comparison. Level 2 (2-3): compares content, agreement OR disagreement, with details. Level 3 (4-5): compares agreement AND disagreement with details. Level 4 (6-7): compares the overall messages / points of view, supported, and explains why they differ (provenance). [7] (c) Level 1 (1): undeveloped or generic comment. Level 2 (2-3): useful or not useful based on face-value content. Level 3 (4-5): uses content checked against own knowledge. Level 4 (6-7): evaluates the provenance (author, audience, purpose, date) to judge usefulness. [7]

items.stem: Read this student's answer to the question ‘The alliance system was the main cause of the First World War.’ “Alliances turned a quarrel between Austria-Hungary and Serbia into a war between the Great Powers within a week. The blank cheque and the Franco-Russian alliance meant each power felt obliged to act.” Using the levels (L3 explains one side; L4 explains both sides; L5 explains both sides with a supported judgement), which level does it reach? Explain your decision.
items.answer: Level 3 (4-6 marks): it explains one side of the argument only.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct level; 1 mark for a justification referring to the descriptors [2]

items.stem: A student is planning an answer to: ‘Military force was the main way the USSR controlled eastern Europe.’ They have written these points in support: Soviet troops crushed uprisings in East Germany (1953) and Hungary (1956). The Warsaw Pact justified stationing troops in satellite states. Give two explained counter-arguments that the student could use.
items.answer: Loyal communist parties governed day to day. Secret police and censorship kept people in line.

items.stem: A student is planning an answer to: ‘The Treaty of Versailles was fair given the situation in 1919.’ They have written these points in support: France and Belgium had suffered great destruction and needed compensation. items.stem: Here is a student's answer to the question “Describe the Fourteen Points that dealt with territory in Europe.” [4]: “Serbia to be given access to the sea. Belgium to be evacuated and restored. This was a big event in history. The war became a stalemate near the 38th parallel until the armistice of July 1953.” Using the mark scheme (one mark per relevant point, a further mark for supporting detail), how many marks would you award? Explain your decision and suggest how the answer could be improved.
items.answer: 2 marks: 2 relevant points with no further development; the general sentence and the point about a different topic gain no credit. To improve, add further precise points such as: Alsace-Lorraine to be returned to France. Italy's frontiers to follow clear lines of nationality.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct mark (2/4); 1 mark for explaining why the other sentences gain no credit; 1 mark for a valid improvement with accurate detail [3]

items.stem: Practise your (a) technique. What reforms were introduced during the Prague Spring?
items.answer: Censorship was relaxed and the press could criticise the government. People were allowed more freedom to travel abroad. Some private enterprise and more trade with the West. Greater power for trade unions and less central planning. Discussion of other political groups, though the Communist Party kept the leading role.
items.markingKey: One mark for each relevant point; a further mark for supporting detail, up to 4 marks. Indicative content: Censorship was relaxed and the press could criticise the government. People were allowed more freedom to travel abroad. Some private enterprise and more trade with the West. Greater power for trade unions and less central planning. Discussion of other political groups, though the Communist Party kept the leading role. [4]

items.stem: What is meant by “short-term cause”?
options: Checking a source against other sources and own knowledge.
A cause that happened shortly before an event and made it more likely to happen then.
Name or state a point briefly, without needing to explain it.
Give a detailed account of the main features of an event or situation, with accurate supporting detail.
items.answer: A cause that happened shortly before an event and made it more likely to happen then.
items.markingKey: Short-term cause: a cause that happened shortly before an event and made it more likely to happen then. [1]

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “There is no butter, no meat and hardly any potatoes. Sailors from Kiel have come with red flags and the Kaiser has gone. People say the war is lost, yet our soldiers are still standing in France.” (An extract from the diary of a Berlin housewife, November 1918 (illustrative, based on typical accounts).) Explain the difference between the message of Source A and its purpose, using details of the source.
items.answer: Message: It suggests Germany was hungry, in revolution and that people were confused because the army had not been beaten on German soil. Purpose: To record daily life privately during the revolution, so it was not written to persuade others.

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “The peoples of Austria-Hungary, whose place among the nations we wish to see safeguarded and assured, should be accorded the freest opportunity to autonomous development.” (Point 10 of President Wilson's Fourteen Points, January 1918.) Explain the difference between the message of Source A and its purpose, using details of the source.
items.answer: Message: Wilson wanted the nationalities of Austria-Hungary to be allowed to govern themselves. Purpose: To support the national groups of Austria-Hungary and weaken the enemy alliance.

items.stem: Source skills practice: cross-referencing. Source A: a British cartoon published in Punch magazine in October 1912. The cartoon shows the leaders of the Great Powers sitting on the lid of a large pot labelled “Balkan Troubles”, which is boiling over, as they try to keep the lid down. Source B: an extract from a history book written in 2014 (illustrative extract by an unnamed historian). “No government in 1914 deliberately planned a general European war. But the alliances, and the railway timetables of mobilisation tied to them, meant that a local quarrel in the Balkans became a continental war within six weeks.” (a) What can you infer from each source about the causes of the First World War? [4] (b) How far do Sources A and B agree? [7] (c) Which source is more useful to a historian studying the causes of the First World War? Explain your answer using the provenance of both sources. [7]
items.answer: (a) A: The cartoonist suggests the Balkans was a dangerous problem that the Great Powers were struggling to contain, and that it could “boil over” into a wider war. B: The historian argues that the alliances and mobilisation plans turned a local crisis into a general war. (b) They disagree about whether the alliance system was the main cause of the First World War. (c) A: it was published at the time, during the Balkan Wars, and reflects how informed opinion in Britain saw the danger; but it is one magazine's view; it simplifies a complex situation and was produced to comment, not to explain the causes in detail. B: it is written with hindsight by someone who can use evidence from all the countries involved; but it is one interpretation and the extract is short; other historians place more blame on Germany. Judgement depends on the enquiry; each is useful for different purposes.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks for each valid inference supported from the source [4] (b) Level 1 (1): undeveloped comparison. Level 2 (2-3): compares content, agreement OR disagreement, with details. Level 3 (4-5): compares agreement AND disagreement with details. Level 4 (6-7): compares the overall messages / points of view, supported, and explains why they differ (provenance). [7] (c) Level 1 (1): undeveloped or generic comment. Level 2 (2-3): useful or not useful based on face-value content. Level 3 (4-5): uses content checked against own knowledge. Level 4 (6-7): evaluates the provenance (author, audience, purpose, date) to judge usefulness. [7]
